Family Health

Unexpected vaginal bleeding: possible causes and when to get help

Updated: October 5, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Blood between expected periods can range from a few spots to a heavier flow. Hormonal contraception is one possible explanation, but infection, cervical changes, pregnancy-related problems and other conditions can also cause bleeding. The amount, timing, symptoms and possibility of pregnancy help determine what to do next. Colour alone cannot show whether bleeding is harmless.

Check first for symptoms that need urgent care

Seek emergency help for very heavy bleeding, fainting, collapse, severe abdominal or pelvic pain, or bleeding with marked dizziness or breathlessness. If pregnancy is possible, bleeding with one-sided pain or shoulder-tip pain can signal an ectopic pregnancy and needs urgent assessment. Do not wait for a positive home test if these symptoms occur.

During a known pregnancy, contact your maternity or early-pregnancy service promptly about any bleeding, including light spotting. Heavy bleeding that rapidly soaks a pad, severe pain or feeling faint requires immediate care. The appropriate local service depends on where you live and how far along the pregnancy is.

Someone using estrogen-containing contraception should also seek urgent care for chest pain, sudden breathing difficulty, severe leg pain or swelling, or new neurological or visual symptoms. These are not ordinary signs of breakthrough bleeding and should not be left for a routine follow-up.

Spotting, periods and breakthrough bleeding

Spotting usually means a small amount of blood noticed on underwear or toilet paper, often without needing the protection used for a period. A heavier flow may require a pad or another menstrual product. Pink, red and brown blood can occur with several causes; brown often reflects older blood but does not establish the diagnosis.

A menstrual cycle is counted from the first day of one period to the first day of the next. A 28-day cycle with ovulation around day 14 is an example, not a timetable everyone follows. Cycle length, the timing of ovulation and the number of bleeding days vary.

The uterine lining changes in response to hormones. When pregnancy does not occur, hormone changes normally lead to shedding of the lining as a period. Hormonal contraception can alter this pattern, and a scheduled withdrawal bleed on a pill is not the same as a natural menstrual period.

Cycles may be less predictable in adolescence and around perimenopause, but heavy or persistent unexpected bleeding still deserves assessment. Average estimates of blood loss, sometimes expressed as a few tablespoons, are difficult to apply at home. Describe flooding, clots, product changes and the effect on daily life instead.

The term breakthrough bleeding is often used for unscheduled bleeding with hormonal contraception. Bleeding in pregnancy should be assessed as pregnancy-related bleeding, rather than assumed to be the same harmless adjustment.

1. Starting or changing hormonal contraception

Unscheduled spotting can happen with pills, implants, injections, hormonal IUDs, patches or vaginal rings. It is often more noticeable during the first months of a new method, and the longer-term pattern depends on the method and the individual.

Bleeding can reflect changes in the uterine lining while using hormones. It is not evidence that the body needs to clear out accumulated blood, and spotting alone does not mean that contraception has failed.

Missed or late pills can affect both bleeding and pregnancy protection. Vomiting or significant diarrhoea may interfere with absorption of an oral pill, while certain medicines or supplements can reduce its effectiveness. The correct response depends on the exact pill, the timing and the interacting product.

Check the product’s missed-pill or illness instructions and ask a pharmacist or clinician promptly if you are unsure. Additional contraception or emergency contraception may be relevant in some situations. Do not assume that every antibiotic interacts or that any episode of spotting means pregnancy.

Smoking is associated with more breakthrough bleeding in some hormonal-contraceptive users, but it does not explain every episode or justify ignoring new symptoms. Support with stopping smoking can benefit health; bleeding still needs its own assessment when indicated.

Extended-cycle pills and continuous use

Some regimens use active pills for longer than the usual monthly cycle, reducing how often a withdrawal bleed occurs. Others use hormones continuously. Examples include combined pills containing ethinyl estradiol and levonorgestrel, but schedules and formulations differ.

Spotting is common early in extended or continuous use and may improve over time. It can be red or brown and may come and go. A longer regimen is not automatically unsafe because there is no monthly bleed, and blood does not have to build up inside the uterus.

If the pattern is troublesome, a clinician can check for other causes and discuss a suitable adjustment or alternative method. Do not create an unscheduled pill-free break without instructions: its timing can affect pregnancy protection. The solution should fit the specific method and your preferences.

Hormonal and copper IUDs have different bleeding patterns

A hormonal IUD releases progestogen and often causes irregular spotting at first; bleeding commonly becomes lighter over time. A copper IUD contains no hormones and can make periods heavier or longer, especially in the early months. Both can be associated with bleeding between periods.

The difference matters: copper-IUD bleeding is not caused by an influx of new hormones. New bleeding after a previously settled pattern, persistent troublesome bleeding or bleeding after sex should not automatically be attributed to the device.

Contact a clinician for heavy bleeding, pelvic pain, fever, unusual discharge or concern that an IUD has moved. If pregnancy is possible, take that possibility seriously even though IUDs are highly effective. Assessment may include a pregnancy test and checking the device’s position.

2. Infection or inflammation

Sexually transmitted infections such as chlamydia and gonorrhoea can cause inflammation of the cervix and bleeding between periods or after sex. They may also have few or no symptoms. Bleeding does not prove that an STI is present, and an infection cannot be identified from appearance alone.

Other relevant conditions include cervicitis, meaning inflammation of the cervix; endometritis, involving the uterine lining; vaginitis, involving the vagina; and pelvic inflammatory disease, which affects the upper reproductive tract. These conditions do not all have the same cause or treatment, and not every one is sexually transmitted.

Pelvic discomfort, burning when passing urine, unusual discharge or a new odour can be clues. Cloudy urine alone is nonspecific and may point to a urinary issue rather than a genital infection. Tell the clinician about the full pattern, including recent sexual contact and whether pregnancy is possible.

Bacterial infections may need antibiotics selected for the likely or confirmed cause. Use prescribed treatment rather than leftover antibiotics or vaginal products chosen by guesswork. Depending on the diagnosis, partners may need testing or treatment too.

Untreated pelvic inflammatory disease can lead to chronic pain, fertility problems or a higher risk of ectopic pregnancy. Prompt assessment matters. Severe pain, fever, vomiting, heavy bleeding or feeling very unwell requires urgent help.

3. A cervix that bleeds when irritated

The cervix is the lower part of the uterus opening into the vagina. Its surface can sometimes bleed after sex or an examination. A common benign change called cervical ectropion makes more delicate cells visible on the outer surface, where contact may cause spotting.

During pregnancy, changes in the cervix and its blood supply can make contact bleeding more likely. That is a possible explanation, not one that can safely be assumed at home. Report bleeding in pregnancy so the care team can decide what assessment is needed.

Infection, a polyp, injury or less commonly a precancerous or cancerous change can also cause cervical bleeding. Repeated bleeding after sex should be checked even if previous cervical screening was normal.

Cervical insufficiency is a different issue: the cervix can shorten or open too early during pregnancy, sometimes with few symptoms. It is not simply a sensitive cervix and cannot be diagnosed from spotting alone. New pelvic pressure, fluid leakage, cramps or bleeding in pregnancy should be discussed promptly with maternity care.

4. A subchorionic haematoma in pregnancy

A subchorionic haematoma is a collection of blood between the uterine wall and the membranes around the pregnancy, or later beneath the placenta. It is thought to involve a degree of separation at that boundary. It may cause spotting, heavier bleeding or clots, and sometimes is found on a scan without any bleeding.

An ultrasound can help identify the collection and assess the pregnancy. Bleeding alone cannot tell you its size or location, and not every collection is visible on the first scan.

Many affected pregnancies continue normally and the collection resolves. However, the finding is not a guarantee that there is no risk. Size, location, stage of pregnancy and other circumstances can influence the follow-up plan.

The care team may recommend observation or repeat scanning when appropriate. Ask what to do if bleeding continues or worsens. Do not assume that a particular activity restriction, supplement or home remedy will remove the collection; follow the individual plan you are given.

5. Miscarriage or ectopic pregnancy

Bleeding in pregnancy does not always mean pregnancy loss, but miscarriage is one possible cause. It may involve spotting or a heavier flow, cramps, clots or passage of tissue. Some losses are diagnosed on ultrasound without obvious bleeding. Definitions of miscarriage use different gestational limits in different health systems, so a single week cutoff should not guide whether to seek care.

If miscarriage is confirmed, options can include waiting under an agreed plan, medicines or a procedure to remove pregnancy tissue. Surgical treatment may use suction and is sometimes described as dilation and curettage, or D&C. It is not necessary for every miscarriage or every episode of prolonged bleeding.

Bleeding or spotting can continue for around two weeks after a miscarriage and sometimes longer, depending on the situation and treatment. The team should explain the expected course and follow-up. Increasing bleeding, fever, worsening pain, faintness or feeling unwell should prompt reassessment rather than being accepted as routine recovery.

An ectopic pregnancy develops outside the main uterine cavity, most often in a fallopian tube. It cannot continue safely there and can cause dangerous internal bleeding if it ruptures. Symptoms may include unusual vaginal bleeding, one-sided abdominal pain, shoulder-tip pain, dizziness or collapse.

Treatment is not always surgery. Carefully selected stable cases may be managed with close monitoring or medicine such as methotrexate; other cases need an operation, urgently if rupture is suspected. These decisions require specialist assessment and follow-up, not symptom-based self-treatment.

6. Fibroids and other uterine growths

Fibroids are non-cancerous growths in or around the uterus. They can be associated with heavy, prolonged or irregular bleeding, although many cause no symptoms. Hormones and family history play a role, and having a close relative with fibroids increases the likelihood.

Fibroids are reported more often in some populations, including Black women. This is a population pattern rather than a way to diagnose an individual or a reason to dismiss symptoms in anyone else.

Possible symptoms include periods lasting longer than a week, pelvic pressure or pain, frequent urination, difficulty emptying the bladder, constipation, lower-back discomfort or pain that can extend toward the legs. These symptoms are not specific to fibroids.

An examination and ultrasound can help identify the size and position of fibroids. Treatment depends on symptoms, bleeding, fertility plans and the findings. Small symptom-free fibroids may need no active treatment. Polyps and other uterine conditions can also cause bleeding, so a presumed fibroid should not end the investigation prematurely.

Can spotting tell you that implantation has occurred?

Light bleeding around the time a period is due is sometimes described as implantation bleeding. Early pregnancy is one possible context for spotting, but timing, colour and amount cannot reliably identify the biological cause.

There is no dependable rule that spotting ten to fourteen days after conception proves implantation. Ovulation and conception dates are often uncertain, and contraceptive spotting, an approaching period and other causes can look similar.

A home pregnancy test can detect pregnancy hormone when used at the appropriate time, but it does not prove that bleeding came from implantation or show where the pregnancy is located. An early negative result may need repeating according to the test instructions. Persistent symptoms or a positive test with bleeding warrants clinical advice.

Do not let the label implantation bleeding delay care for pain, dizziness, heavy bleeding or other warning signs. A reassuring colour or small amount cannot rule out ectopic pregnancy.

Practical steps while arranging advice

Record when the bleeding started, how it compares with your usual pattern, whether it followed sex, the products needed and any clots or associated symptoms. Include the last period, contraception, missed doses, new medicines and the possibility of pregnancy.

A pad can make it easier to observe the amount. If pregnancy-related bleeding or miscarriage is possible, use pads and follow the care team’s advice about internal menstrual products. For confirmed uncomplicated contraceptive spotting, a usual menstrual product may be suitable, but it does not treat the cause.

Keep taking contraception according to its instructions unless a clinician advises a change, and seek method-specific advice after missed doses or illness. Avoid taking extra hormones or trying a drug solely to stop unexplained bleeding.

Not every episode can be prevented. The useful next step is to identify the cause, then choose treatment or observation with a clinician. Recurrent bleeding, bleeding after sex or a change after a stable pattern should be reviewed even when the flow is light.

Bleeding after menopause needs assessment

Bleeding after menopause should be checked, even if it happens only once or is just a small amount of spotting. Menopause is usually recognised after twelve months without a natural period, with interpretation adjusted when medicines or other conditions affect bleeding.

Common explanations include thinning of vaginal or uterine tissue, polyps or changes associated with hormone therapy. A thickened uterine lining or cancer is less common but important to investigate. It is not appropriate to assume that the cause is infection or an underactive thyroid.

Assessment may include an examination, ultrasound and sometimes a sample of the uterine lining. A small amount of blood does not make that assessment unnecessary. Contact a clinician promptly rather than waiting to see whether several more episodes occur.

What an assessment may involve

A clinician will ask about your usual cycle, pregnancy possibility, contraception, medicines, sexual-health concerns and other symptoms. Depending on the situation, tests may include a pregnancy test, blood count for anaemia, infection testing, an examination or ultrasound.

An internal examination should be explained and done with your consent. You can ask for a chaperone, raise concerns about discomfort and ask for it to stop. The appropriate tests depend on the likely cause; everyone does not need every investigation.

Some contraceptive spotting settles with time, while infection, fibroids or pregnancy complications need a different plan. Agree on follow-up and the symptoms that should bring you back sooner. The goal is to understand the change and manage it safely, not simply suppress bleeding without explanation.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

NHS guidance advises assessment of bleeding between periods, after sex and after menopause. Pregnancy bleeding requires prompt advice, with emergency care for heavy bleeding, severe pain, shoulder pain or faintness.

ACOG and CDC guidance recognise method-specific bleeding changes with contraception. Miscarriage and ectopic pregnancy have several management options; choice depends on diagnosis, symptoms and clinical findings.

How BeMama can help

Use a private cycle or symptom note to record timing, amount, pain and contraception details for your appointment. A predicted cycle phase cannot diagnose implantation, miscarriage or the cause of bleeding.

When to seek help

Get emergency help for heavy bleeding with faintness, severe pain or breathing difficulty. Bleeding with shoulder-tip or one-sided abdominal pain when pregnancy is possible needs urgent assessment. Report all pregnancy bleeding and any bleeding after menopause.

Evidence notes updated: October 5, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Spotting describes an amount of blood, not its cause.
  • Contraceptive bleeding patterns vary by method and do not alone show contraceptive failure.
  • Pregnancy bleeding needs advice even when it is light.
  • A pregnancy test cannot establish that bleeding came from implantation.
  • Miscarriage and ectopic pregnancy do not always require surgery.
  • Bleeding after menopause should be checked even after one small episode.

Frequently asked questions

Is brown spotting always harmless old blood?

Brown often reflects older blood, but colour does not establish the cause or exclude a problem.

Does breakthrough bleeding mean my contraception stopped working?

Not by itself. Missed pills, vomiting, diarrhoea or certain interactions can separately affect protection, so check the instructions for your method.

Can I take a pill-free break to stop continuous-pill spotting?

Only follow a suitable plan from the product instructions or clinician. An improvised break can reduce protection, depending on its timing.

Do copper IUDs cause bleeding because of hormones?

No. Copper IUDs contain no hormones, although they can cause heavier periods or spotting. Hormonal IUDs have a different bleeding pattern.

Can an infection cause bleeding without obvious discharge?

Yes. Some infections have few symptoms. Testing and assessment are more reliable than judging by discharge or blood colour.

Does bleeding in pregnancy always mean miscarriage?

No, but it should be reported promptly. Some causes need urgent treatment and cannot be identified at home.

Does a subchorionic haematoma always cause pregnancy loss?

No. Many resolve and the pregnancy continues normally. Follow-up depends on the findings and symptoms.

Does ectopic pregnancy always need surgery?

No. Selected stable cases may have close monitoring or medicine. Rupture or other concerning findings may require emergency surgery.

Can a positive home test confirm implantation bleeding?

No. It detects pregnancy hormone but does not identify the bleeding source or the pregnancy’s location.

Should I report one small spot of blood after menopause?

Yes. Even a single light episode should be assessed, although many causes are benign.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
